current_episode.title: Helping Business Owners Navigate Legal Challenges with Confidence (Brian Calhoun (Managing Partner) & Blake Brownshadel (Partner), Calhoun Bhella LLP)

guest.bio_context: Brian Calhoun started practicing law in California before moving to Dallas, where he worked as a young associate and senior associate at big law firms. In 2010, he founded Calhoun Bhella LLP with partner Gwen Bella, initially focusing on litigation before expanding into transactional practice. His specialty is helping entrepreneurs and business owners with acquisitions, sales, corporate matters, vendor contracts, and employment agreements.

Hi, this is Gene Bohensky with another episode of the Think Small Podcast. And today we have Brian Calhoun and Blake Brown-Shaddle with Calhoun Bella, which is a full-service law firm. They specialize in litigation and transactional matters for business owners and entrepreneurs. So, welcome, guys. Brian, let's get started. Tell me about you and your background. Thanks, Gene. Yes. So my background, I started practicing law out in California originally and moved back to Dallas and was working as a young associate and then more senior associate, big firms, both in California and in Dallas. In 2010, I decided to start with another one of my partners, Gwen Bella, the firm Calhoun Bella. And we started this firm, and the idea was to focus on those entrepreneurs and business owners for their various legal matters. Initially, it was only litigation, and then we started to add the transactional practice, which is where my specialty lies. Mainly in helping people buy and sell businesses is what my practice focuses on. But then also just kind of the general corporate matters, helping people with vendor contracts and third-party contracts and employment agreements, just anything that a normal general counsel does where those mid-sized companies, those mid-market companies that aren't quite big enough to have their own internal general counsel. Right. Interesting. I remember, Vogue, first, you had a couple of interesting things to say about why you started the business and what your approach is. Yeah. You know, when I was at these bigger firms, you know, we were a small line item in these big companies' budgets. It was important for those companies, the stuff that we did for them, the legal work that we did, but not like these entrepreneurs and these smaller businesses that we represent at Calhoun Bella. You know, it's great to be able to focus on their legal matters because it means so much more. At least this is what we're seeing as we see that it means so much more to them from what we do, both on the transactional side and the litigation side. We're interacting directly with those business owners or those decision makers. And it's just a lot more fulfilling than a lot of the work that I was doing at these big firms. Interesting. I know Blake had an interesting story to tell how he got involved. Well, thank you. Tell me a bit about yourself. Yeah, sure. I have been practicing law for 16 years, entirely complex commercial litigation, state and federal court across the country. I'm licensed in Texas and New York. But when I got started, well, let me back up. I was originally a neurobiology undergrad student. I wanted to go to med school. And, you know, life kind of leads you in a different direction. And I found that I wanted to go to law school. I wanted to become a lawyer. I wanted to be a litigator for the same reasons that I wanted to be a doctor, which was to take people's problems and issues and concerns and make them my own and solve them and help people. And I was just my brain was just wired for law instead of medicine. So I went to UT Law in Austin, graduated in 2010, went and worked at one of the biggest firms in the world for seven years. And right from the outset, I wanted to be in the courtroom and work with the clients. And it's tough to do that sometimes as a young associate at a big firm where you have institutional clients. So the benefit, the silver lining was I had incredible mentors and incredible experience, and I got to work on some amazing cases. But I got a recruiter in 2017, and that's how I met Brian. And Brian and I went to lunch, and we hit it off immediately because we were like-minded in the notion of how we wanted to grow this firm. pending_qa.q: What is the impact of using ChatGPT to review transactional documents during deal negotiations?
pending_qa.r: When clients use ChatGPT to review contract documents before attorney response, the tool often generates 10 to 20 issues or questions, but typically only two or three are valid insights the attorney wasn't already planning to address. This creates additional attorney time and expense as lawyers must address both the opposing side's document and respond to non-substantive matters AI raises, ultimately increasing client costs and potentially delaying deal closure.

pending_qa.q: What disclosure requirements are courts implementing regarding AI-generated legal documents?
pending_qa.r: One court in Fort Worth recently amended local rules to require that if any part of a document being filed contains AI-generated content, it must be disclosed on the front. This requirement exists because courts want to distinguish between content prepared by licensed attorneys versus content generated by AI systems, as relying on undisclosed AI content can result in loss of credibility.
